entities.name: Poetic Edda
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Poetic Edda, a foundational text of Old Norse literature, emerged in medieval Iceland around the late 13th century, although it encompasses oral traditions dating back centuries earlier. This collection of anonymous narrative poems is crucial for understanding the mythology, history, and culture of the Norse people. It encapsulates tales of gods, heroes, and the creation of the world, providing invaluable insights into the beliefs and values that shaped Norse society. Key figures such as Odin and Thor, and significant locations like Asgard, feature prominently in these narratives, which have influenced not just literature but also modern interpretations of Viking history.

The Poetic Edda consists of 31 poems preserved in the Codex Regius manuscript, which was likely compiled in the 13th century. Among its most notable works are 'Völuspá,' which outlines the creation and eventual destruction of the world, and 'Hávamál,' a collection of wisdom and maxims attributed to Odin. These poems were not merely literary works; they served as a cultural repository, preserving the mythology and ethos of a society transitioning from paganism to Christianity. The text's existence illustrates the synthesis of oral and written traditions, as well as the socio-political context of medieval Iceland, which was marked by chieftainships and the establishment of a unique literary culture.

The legacy of the Poetic Edda extends far beyond its original audience, influencing later Scandinavian literature and the broader field of mythology studies. It has inspired countless authors, poets, and artists, from Richard Wagner in the 19th century to modern fantasy writers like J.R.R. Tolkien. The Edda has been instrumental in reviving interest in Norse mythology during the Romantic period and continues to be a touchstone for discussions about cultural identity in Scandinavia. Its themes resonate in contemporary popular culture, showcasing the enduring power of these ancient narratives.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Poetic Edda (Old Norse: Edda; also known as the Elder Edda or Sæmundar Edda, though neither attribution is accurate) is a collection of Old Norse mythological and heroic poems preserved primarily in the Codex Regius manuscript (Konungsbók, 'King's Book'), a vellum codex written c. 1270 CE in Iceland, donated to the Danish King Frederick III in 1662 and now in the Árni Magnússon Institute for Icelandic Studies, Reykjavik. The Codex Regius contains 29 poems; additional poems from other manuscripts are conventionally included in editions of the Poetic Edda, bringing the total to approximately 34–40 poems depending on the edition. The poems are thought to have been composed between the 9th and 13th centuries CE, with some possibly preserving material of considerably greater antiquity.

The Poetic Edda falls into two groups: mythological poems (Völuspá, 'The Seeress's Prophecy' — a cosmological narrative from the creation of the world to Ragnarök and the new world after; Hávamál, 'Words of the High One' — wisdom poetry attributed to Odin; Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál, Skírnismál, Lokasenna, Þrymskviða, and others dealing with Norse gods — Odin, Thor, Freyr, Loki) and heroic poems (the Sigurd cycle — Reginsmál, Fáfnismál, Sigrdrífumál, Atlakviða, Atlamál, and others — dealing with the legend of Sigurd the dragon-slayer and the Nibelungen material that also underlies the German Nibelungenlied).
